tier_reason: The 2M reference report compares ZoneTree against RocksDB and SQLite, plus MySQL, with matching checksums across engines. It states the CPU (AMD EPYC 4345P), OS and .NET 10.0.9. The benchmark code is public at benchmarks/profile-store/src (ProfileStore.Benchmark.csproj, BenchmarkRunner.cs, RocksDbProfileStore.cs, SqliteProfileStore.cs), and its README gives the build and run settings: dotnet run -c Release, Server GC, DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0 for reference runs.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Total run time 181,390 ms (ZoneTree) vs 429,036 ms (RocksDB, ~2.4x faster, derived from page data) vs 1,062,037 ms (SQLite, ~5.9x faster, derived from page data). Lookup by email: 388,867/s (ZoneTree) vs 138,471/s (RocksDB) vs 277,620/s (SQLite). Read by user id: 970,010/s vs 272,133/s (RocksDB) vs 404,469/s (SQLite). The raw insert phase is a tie with RocksDB (182,070/s vs 181,662/s). Once the post-insert stabilization is counted, RocksDB's insert-ready throughput (154,360/s) is ahead of ZoneTree's (141,281/s).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: .NET 10.0.9 (net10.0, C# 14), dotnet run -c Release, Server GC. The benchmark policy says reference runs set DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0.
corrections.caveats: Several reference sizes are published (100K to 100M profiles, plus Windows 11 p1/p16 runs). The numbers above come from the 2M-profile Linux report only. The benchmark is a single custom profile-store workload, and the project explicitly warns against generalizing it. The RocksDB baseline is RocksDbSharp/RocksDbNative 6.2.2, an old RocksDB release reached through C# P/Invoke. It runs as five separate RocksDB instances with application-managed secondary indexes and no cross-index WriteBatch. SQLite (3.50.3 via Microsoft.Data.Sqlite) does single-row autocommit writes with synchronous=NORMAL, which is why its insert and update phases are slow. Durability settings differ: ZoneTree uses an async compressed WAL, while RocksDB uses a WAL with unsynced writes. ZoneTree's peak process memory (3.3 GB) is about 3x RocksDB's (1.1 GB). The repo now lives at github.com/ZoneTree/ZoneTree, and koculu/ZoneTree redirects there.

notes: Every quoted number matches the 2M report. The only wording error was calling 154,360/s RocksDB's 'raw insert throughput': that figure is its insert-plus-stabilize readiness throughput, and the raw insert phase is effectively tied. Metadata checks out: MIT, 504 stars, last commit 2026-09-15, not a fork, not archived. The canonical owner is now the ZoneTree org.

tier_reason: The README table compares SurrealKV directly with RocksDB on a named CPU (Threadripper 9970X), and every quoted ratio matches. The harness, crud-bench, is SurrealDB's own tool, not an independent third-party suite, so B does not apply. It is not A either, because the README gives no Rust toolchain or build flags, and no crud-bench commit or engine versions for the run.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 3.31x faster creates (105,072 vs 31,777 OPS), 3.08x faster updates, 2.84x faster deletes, 2.31x faster point reads (1,602,668 vs 692,597 OPS) and 3.47x faster range scans (8,361 vs 2,406 OPS) vs RocksDB. It also beats Fjall and SlateDB. LMDB (27,446 OPS) and Libmdbx (16,005 OPS) beat it on range scans, and RocksDB has the lowest peak memory (393 MB vs SurrealKV's 1.35 GB).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the SurrealKV README. The crud-bench Cargo.toml release profile uses lto=true, opt-level=3, codegen-units=1 and panic=abort, with rust-version >= 1.91.0. The toolchain actually used is not stated.
corrections.caveats: crud-bench is maintained by SurrealDB, the same org as SurrealKV, so despite covering many engines it is not independent. Its RocksDB adapter uses SurrealDB's own fork crate (surrealdb-rocksdb 0.24.0-surreal.5), with configuration chosen by SurrealDB. The README does not record the crud-bench commit, SurrealKV version or Rust toolchain behind its numbers: crud-bench main pins surrealkv 0.21.2, while the workspace is at 0.21.4. SurrealKV's peak memory (1.35 GB) is well above RocksDB's (393 MB).

notes: All README numbers and ratios check out. The downgrade is only a tier fix: the record rated first-party crud-bench as B, but same-org harness numbers with unstated toolchain and flags are C. Metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 554 stars, last commit 2026-09-26, active.

tier_reason: The numbers are first-party, from the AnuDBBenchmark README (anusqlite_benchmark.cpp) on an unnamed Raspberry Pi. The build script gives no -O level, and the SQLite and RocksDB static-lib flags are unstated, so at most C. On substance, SQLite wins insert, update and delete by 2.1-5.3x, and neither 'win' holds up. In the parallel test AnuDB took 1.71x longer wall time (1429 s vs 835 s), and SQLite's op count is cut because 3 of its 4 threads failed to commit (no busy_timeout, contended transactions). The 1.23x query 'win' has AnuDB returning only doc IDs while SQLite reads the json_data column of every row.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No valid speedup vs SQLite3. The page's only 'wins' are a 1.23x query ops/s edge (34.38 vs 27.89 ops/s, where AnuDB returns doc IDs only and SQLite reads json_data) and a 2.34x parallel ops/s ratio (6.996 vs 2.992 ops/s). In that parallel run both engines used 4 threads, AnuDB took 1429 s vs SQLite's 835 s, and SQLite completed only 2,500 of 10,000 ops because 3 of its 4 threads failed to commit. SQLite3 is 3.9x faster on inserts, 2.1x faster on updates and 5.3x faster on deletes.
corrections.hardware: Raspberry Pi. The README leaves the model unspecified; the May 2025 Show HN post, describing an earlier run with different numbers, says Raspberry Pi 2 (ARMv7).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: build_anusqlite.sh: rpi-tools arm-bcm2708 arm-linux-gnueabihf-g++ -std=c++11, with no optimization level given, linked against prebuilt static libsqlite3.a and librocksdb.a whose build flags are unstated.
corrections.caveats: The Show HN title (item 43903414, 2025-05-06) claimed '279x Faster Than SQLite in Parallel Workloads'. That came from an earlier run with 10 threads (AnuDB 412 vs SQLite 1.4 ops/s) that is no longer on the benchmark page. The current page shows a 2.34x parallel ops/s ratio, and the record's '10 threads vs SQLite3's 4' is wrong: the comparison code uses NUM_THREADS=4 for both engines, and the 10-thread output is an AnuDB-only example run. The parallel ratio comes from SQLite's lock failures (3 of 4 threads failed to commit), not a like-for-like throughput win. SQLite wins insert, update and delete outright. The AnuDBBenchmark repo has no license file.

notes: Rejected as not-faster on invalidity grounds, as with fastestjsoninthewest: the numbers are on the page, but the two 'wins' come from a broken SQLite harness (failed commits; AnuDB slower by wall time) and asymmetric query work, and SQLite wins the rest. If the orchestrator keeps it under the flagged-entries policy, use tier C with the corrected claimed_speedup and caveats. Metadata checks out: MIT, 56 stars, last commit 2025-06-24 (stale).
